subtype: Approach: linking each item to a place in the house [Thinking]
passage: On the way home from the village school, Usha listened to her teacher's list in her head: glue bottle, scissors, chart paper. At home, Nazia was waiting in the yard. "How will you remember three things till tomorrow?" Usha closed her eyes. "I'm walking through our house. The glue bottle is stuck on the front door, so I can't get in. The scissors are on the sofa, snipping the cushion. And the chart paper is on the fridge, flapping like a flag." She opened her eyes. "Door, sofa, fridge." Nazia laughed. The next morning Usha packed all three at once without a single pause.

qa.q: Where did Usha picture the glue bottle?
qa.a: Usha pictured the glue bottle on the front door.

qa.q: Why did Usha imagine the items in odd places?
qa.a: Usha found the silly pictures easier to remember, and felt confident that walking through the house in her mind would bring each item back. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Usha use, and why?
qa.a: Usha could write the three items on her hand or a slip of paper, or ask a parent to remind her. A written note works even on a tired day.

qa.q: How does Nazia see Usha's method?
qa.a: Nazia asked how three things could be remembered and laughed at the pictures, so Nazia finds it funny and clever, and may want to try it.

grounding: A child imagines a glue bottle on the door, scissors on the sofa and chart paper on the fridge, and walking through the house in her mind brings each item back.

subtype: Approach: linking each item to a place in the house [Thinking]
passage: Astrid's teacher in Uppsala had listed five things for Monday's art project, and Astrid had no pen. On the walk home she thought, "Put each one somewhere in the house." She pictured a glue stick stuck right across the front door. Scissors snipping at the sofa cushions. A roll of red paper lying on top of the fridge like a cat. Pipe cleaners curling out of the bath tap. A packet of paints sitting on her own pillow. At dinner her brother Mateo asked what she needed. Astrid closed her eyes and toured the rooms in her head: door, sofa, fridge, bath, bed. "Glue, scissors, red paper, pipe cleaners, paints." Mateo counted on his fingers. Five.

qa.q: Where did Astrid picture the pipe cleaners?
qa.a: She pictured them curling out of the bath tap.

qa.q: How did Astrid probably feel when she named all five things at dinner?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased and confident, since walking through the house in her head worked.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Astrid if she had a pen, and why?
qa.a: Writing the list would be quicker and safer, because paper holds it even if she is tired or distracted.

qa.q: How does Astrid's memory trick look to Mateo?
qa.a: Mateo sees her close her eyes and list everything, so it probably looks impressive and a little mysterious to him.

grounding: It shows a child placing each needed item somewhere in her house in her mind and recalling them by walking through it.

subtype: Approach: linking each item to a place in the house [Thinking]
passage: "Tomorrow's craft: tape, a paper cup, string, a pencil and a button," Jagdish sir said just as the bell rang, and the class burst out of the door. Damini stayed in her seat, eyes shut. "My house," she thought. "Gate first. There's tape stuck across the gate. Then the shoe rack, and a paper cup sitting in Papa's shoe. The kitchen: string tied round the pressure cooker. My desk: a pencil standing in the fan hook. My bed: a big shiny button on the pillow." She opened her eyes. Jagdish sir was watching. "You're not going home?" "I was going home," Damini said. "In my head. Tape, cup, string, pencil, button." He laughed and wrote them on the board anyway.

qa.q: What did Damini picture tied round the pressure cooker?
qa.a: She pictured string tied round the pressure cooker.

qa.q: What was Damini thinking about while her eyes were shut?
qa.a: She was calmly walking through her house in her mind, placing each item in a spot so she would not forget; she seemed focused and sure of herself.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish sir do to support pupils who cannot use this trick?
qa.a: He could give the list earlier, not as the bell rings, and write it on the board, so everyone has time to copy it.

qa.q: How does Damini's answer look to Jagdish sir?
qa.a: He is amused and curious, and writing the list on the board shows he also wants the rest of the class to have it.

grounding: It shows a girl linking each item to a place in her house and recalling them in turn as she imagines walking through it.
